**Plan created (pl_002, active) for q_001 — "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"**

---

### Existing facts the plan builds on

- Patrick Flynn (I1): born ~1845 Ireland; died 1908-03-12 Schuylkill County, PA (death cert. no. 4521)
- Thomas Flynn (I2): born ~1818 Ireland; parent-child relationship R1 (Thomas → Patrick) is sourced from the 1850 census and two other records — all indirect co-residence evidence
- **No mother has been named anywhere in the tree**
- Patrick's 1908 death certificate (S3) is already in the tree but no parent names have been extracted from it — a 1908 PA death cert routinely names both parents, so extraction of S3 is recommended before running new searches

---

### Research plan — 9 items in execution order

| # | Record type | Place / Date | Repository | Note |
|---|-------------|--------------|------------|------|
| pli_004 | Census 1870 | Schuylkill Co., PA | FamilySearch | Thomas ~52; household names wife; free repository first |
| **pli_005** | **Census 1870** | **Schuylkill Co., PA** | **Ancestry** (requested) | Independent index; may catch entries FS missed |
| pli_006 | Census 1880 | Schuylkill Co., PA | FamilySearch | First census to record relationship to head of household |
| pli_007 | Probate | Schuylkill Co., PA 1860–1895 | FamilySearch (browse) | S4 already in tree; Thomas's will would name his wife and Patrick as heir |
| pli_008 | Church – marriage | Schuylkill Co., PA 1842–1895 | FamilySearch | Thomas's marriage — confirms couple, supplies mother's maiden name |
| pli_009 | Church – baptisms (FAN) | Schuylkill Co., PA 1842–1895 | FamilySearch | Siblings born in PA; baptism entries name both parents |
| pli_010 | Church (fallback) | Schuylkill Co., PA 1842–1895 | FamilySearch (browse) | Fallback if pli_008 indexed collection misses the parish |
| pli_011 | Naturalization | Schuylkill Co., PA 1849–1880 | FamilySearch (browse) | Petitions often name the wife; date range set by Thomas's lifespan |
| pli_012 | Land deed | Schuylkill Co., PA 1850–1895 | FamilySearch | PA dower law requires wife's relinquishment, directly naming her |

---

### Next steps

- **Immediate:** Ask the extraction agent to pull parent names from Patrick's 1908 death certificate (S3, already in the tree) — this alone may answer the question.
- **FamilySearch searches:** search-records for pli_004, pli_006–pli_012
- **Ancestry search:** search-external-sites for pli_005 (1870 census on Ancestry)

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable. If Thomas Flynn died between 1870 and 1880, his widow (Patrick's mother) may appear as head or in Patrick's household. If still alive, his wife is listed with relationship 'wife.' Extends the search to the later part of the 1845-1908 window. Search Flynn and variants.

Source S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is already recorded in the project tree but no assertions have been extracted from it — this item executes that browse. Thomas Flynn born ~1818 could have died anywhere from ~1860 to ~1895; the date range is bounded by his plausible lifespan, not Patrick's research window. A will naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence; naming his wife would identify Patrick's mother. The loc_001 locality entry confirms probate records are held by the county Register of Wills from 1811.

FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. This dedicated item targets Thomas Flynn's marriage record in Pennsylvania — the candidate parents' marriage to each other. Their marriage record confirms Thomas and his wife as a couple, supplies the mother's maiden name, and by its date relative to Patrick's ca. 1845 birth corroborates Thomas as father where only census co-residence currently supports that link. Note the limit: the marriage record does not by itself prove Patrick is their child; a record placing Patrick with the parents remains necessary. The loc_001 guide notes the family was likely Roman Catholic and sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese. Search under Flynn and variants (Flinn, Flyn). If the mother's name is found, re-search under her maiden surname for an earlier marriage that would mean this surname is a prior married name, not her birth name.

FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable) — this item targets baptisms of Patrick's siblings born in Pennsylvania after the family immigrated ca. 1845. A sibling's baptism entry names both father (Thomas Flynn) and mother, providing direct evidence of the mother's name. Godparents named in Flynn family baptisms are often kin and are FAN evidence — their surnames may lead to the mother's maiden name or the family's origin in Ireland. This is the required FAN item for a parentage question. Note that Patrick himself was born in Ireland ~1845; his baptism would not appear in Schuylkill County registers. Search under Flynn and variants.

The loc_001 guide notes some church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups. Thomas Flynn (born Ireland ~1818) would have filed a declaration of intention and a naturalization petition after arriving ca. 1845. Pennsylvania naturalization records in this era often name the wife and sometimes list children, giving the wife's name — Patrick's mother. Date range set to 1849-1880, the window within which Thomas would plausibly have naturalized; the upper bound is set by Thomas's lifespan, not Patrick's research window.

A deed executed by Thomas Flynn would require his wife's dower relinquishment under Pennsylvania law, directly naming her — identifying Patrick's mother. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**The next item and why.** pli_006 targets Thomas Flynn's probate/will in Schuylkill County. The catalog check confirms the applicable collection is "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" — browse-only (personCount 0), meaning this must be an image browse of the county's probate dockets rather than a name search. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of parentage and would upgrade the proof summary from "Probable" to "Proved." The date range 1870-1890 is appropriate: Thomas disappears from household records after 1860, making a death sometime in that window plausible.

**What follows it.** Once pli_006 is closed, pl_002's items will all be complete. At that point Add-new mode applies: the proof summary itself flags the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses as unsearched, and a new plan targeting those years — plus any church burial records for Thomas Flynn — would be the natural next round. The church collection returned by the catalog ("Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records," name-searchable) could anchor that follow-on plan alongside the probate browse.

---

The research is working toward establishing who Patrick Flynn's parents were; he was born around 1845 and died in 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Two census records from 1850 and 1860 place him as a child in Thomas Flynn's household, and his 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as his father, though the informant was a son-in-law who may have been repeating family tradition rather than speaking from personal knowledge. Because neither census explicitly states relationships and the death certificate came from a secondary informant, the conclusion sits at "probably" rather than "proved." The one open search that can change that rating is an image browse of Pennsylvania probate records from roughly 1870 to 1890 — dockets and wills recorded in Schuylkill County where Thomas Flynn would likely have died. These records must be browsed page by page because the collection is not name-indexed. If a will or estate file names Patrick as a son, the parentage is proved; if it is not found, census records from 1870 through 1900 and Schuylkill County church burial records would be the next round of searches.

The immediate next step is for search-records to complete the image browse of the Pennsylvania probate records for Schuylkill County, covering 1870 to 1890, under the open plan item pli_006.

output.text_response:
**Plan pl_001 created for q_001 — "Who were the parents of Katharina Seeger (b. c. 1843, Baiersbronn)?"**

---

## What You Need to Know

Katharina was born around 1843 in **Baiersbronn, Württemberg** (now Baden-Württemberg, Germany). Because civil registration in Württemberg didn't begin until 1870, her birth falls entirely in the **church record era**. All surviving church records for Baiersbronn are digitized (browse-only images, not name-searchable) on **Archion**, a paid German archive site.

---

## Research Plan (4 items, in order)

### Step 1 — Württemberg Familienregister (pli_001)
**Where:** Archion | **Date range:** 1800–1875
> This household register lists the entire family — parents and all children — on one spread. Finding the Seeger family unit here gives parents' names, their marriage date, and Katharina's birth year in one efficient step, making the baptism browse in Step 2 fast and direct.

### Step 2 — Taufbuch / Baptism Register (pli_002)
**Where:** Archion | **Date range:** 1840–1848
> Katharina's own baptism entry (~1843) is the **primary original source** naming her parents (and godparents). This is the direct, original record of her birth since no civil registration existed yet.

### Step 3 — Heiratsbuch / Parents' Marriage Register (pli_003)
**Where:** Archion | **Date range:** 1820–1845
> The parents' own wedding record names the **mother's maiden name**, which baptism and household registers typically omit. Confirms the father's identity as well.

### Step 4 — Katharina's Own Marriage Record (pli_004)
**Where:** Archion | **Date range:** 1858–1880
> Württemberg marriage records name the bride's father (and often mother), providing **independent corroboration** of parentage from a different life event and a different record creator. A null result here is still informative.

---

## How to Get Started

1. Go to the **Archion parish page for Baiersbronn**:

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

A sibling's baptism naming Thomas and wife together is direct evidence of the family unit and indirect corroborating evidence for Patrick's parentage. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Plan written and validated. The delegation authorized execution without checking in, so execution is handed off now.

**Mode taken:** Create — new plan for q_001 ("Who were the other children born to Bridget Halloran and her first husband, John Doyle, beyond the one already identified (Ellen Doyle)?")

**Tree facts bearing on the question:**
- Bridget Halloran (I1): birth ~1838, Ireland — no other facts or sources
- John Doyle (I2): no facts or dates recorded
- Ellen Doyle (I3): no facts or dates recorded — sole known child

**Plan pl_001 — 9 items in execution order:**

- pli_001 — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1880, FamilySearch: 1880 census (collection 1417683) is name-searchable and uniquely records relationship to head of household — highest-yield single source for identifying all children living at home
- pli_002 — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, FamilySearch: 1870 census (collection 1438024), name-searchable; Bridget ~32, likely most children at home
- pli_003 — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1860, FamilySearch: 1860 census (collection 1473181), name-searchable; recovers eldest Doyle children who may have left home by later enumerations
- pli_004 — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1900, FamilySearch: 1900 census (collection 1325221), name-searchable; includes column for total children born and living — direct evidence of family size
- pli_005 — church, Schuylkill County PA, 1855–1895, FamilySearch: "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH), name-searchable; PA had no civil birth registration before 1906, so Catholic baptismal registers are the primary birth record
- pli_006 — church, Schuylkill County PA, 1842–1895, FamilySearch (fallback for pli_005): image group 007936751, browse-only (personCount 0); covers parishes not yet indexed
- pli_007 — church (marriage), Schuylkill County PA, 1850–1875, FamilySearch: the couple's marriage record via SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (name-searchable); establishes the union, brackets children's births, confirms Bridget's maiden name, and may surface FAN witnesses
- pli_008 — probate, Schuylkill County PA, 1860–1920, FamilySearch: John Doyle's will or estate administration via image group 007936749 (browse-only, personCount 0); a will naming heirs is the strongest direct evidence of all children; date window sized to John's plausible lifespan
- pli_009 — vital_record (marriages), Schuylkill County PA, 1870–1910, FamilySearch: Doyle children's marriage records via SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (name-searchable) and image group 007936753 (browse-only, personCount 0); marriage records name parents; Ellen Doyle's marriage record anchors the search and may name siblings as witnesses

**Fallback:** pli_006 is activated only if pli_005 does not surface all Doyle baptisms.

**Execution already authorized.** All nine items are FamilySearch — handing to **search-records** for pli_001 through pli_009 as authorized by the delegation.

---

This plan targets the question of who else John Doyle and Bridget Halloran had as children in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, beyond their known daughter Ellen Doyle. Because Pennsylvania did not keep civil birth records before 1906, the plan works from the records that do survive: the federal censuses from 1860 through 1900 (which show children living in the household at enumeration time, with the 1880 census uniquely recording each person's relationship to the head), indexed Catholic baptismal registers, John Doyle's probate or will (which would name all his children as heirs), the couple's own marriage record (to confirm and date the union), and marriage records for Doyle children (which state the parents' names). A browse-only microfilm of church records serves as a fallback for any baptisms not yet indexed.

Search-records will now execute each of the nine FamilySearch items in sequence, starting with the 1880 census household search for John and Bridget Doyle in Schuylkill County.

items.rationale: The 1880 U.S. Census (collection 1417683) is name-searchable and is the highest-priority census for this question because it uniquely records each household member's relationship to the head — the only pre-1900 federal census to do so. John Doyle (or Bridget as head if widowed) would appear with children listed by name, age, sex, birthplace, and relationship. Bridget was born ~1838 and would be approximately 42, with children of various ages still at home.

The 1870 U.S. Census (collection 1438024) is name-searchable. Bridget would be approximately 32 and likely in her peak childbearing years; the household should show the most children still living at home. Cross-referencing 1870 and 1880 enumerations can confirm names across both snapshots.

The 1860 U.S. Census (collection 1473181) is name-searchable. Bridget was born ~1838 and would be approximately 22; any children born before 1860 would appear. Searched after 1870 and 1880 because the family may have had fewer or no children that early, but essential to recover the eldest Doyle children who may have left home by later enumerations.

The 1900 U.S. Census (collection 1325221) is name-searchable and includes a column asking women how many children they bore and how many are still living — the most direct census evidence of total children. Bridget would be approximately 62. Even if widowed, she may appear in a child's household; searching for adult Doyle children in Schuylkill County may also surface siblings not found in earlier enumerations.

Pennsylvania had no civil birth registration before 1906 (locality quirk for this jurisdiction), so Catholic baptismal registers are the primary original birth record. The 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable covering 1708-1985. Search for children with surname Doyle baptized in Schuylkill County, with parents John Doyle and Bridget Halloran, from approximately 1855 to 1895. Name variants to include: Doyle, O'Doyle, and spelling variants of Halloran (Halloran, Hallerin, Holleran).

Image group 007936751 is a browse-only (personCount 0) microfilm of Schuylkill County church records (1842-1895, in English and German). It requires image-by-image review. Activated as a fallback if the indexed collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (pli_005) does not return all Doyle baptisms — particularly for parishes not yet indexed. The locality quirk notes some coal-region church films are browse-only and image-only.

A dedicated search for the marriage of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran. Their marriage record (a) establishes them as a married couple and brackets the date before which no children could be born to the union; (b) confirms Bridget's maiden name as Halloran — which later records may omit; and (c) may name witnesses who are family members (FAN leads). The 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable) covers this period. Note: the couple's marriage alone does not establish that any specific child is theirs — a record placing the child with the parents is still needed.

A will or letters of administration for John Doyle would directly name his children as heirs — the strongest single piece of evidence for identifying all children. 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); the relevant microfilm is image group 007936749 (Schuylkill County probate records, 1851-1930). The date range extends to 1920 because John Doyle's death date is unknown; the window is sized to his plausible lifespan as a man married to a woman born ~1838. Probate records are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 per the locality guide.

Marriage records for children bearing the surname Doyle would name their parents, confirming them as children of John and Bridget and identifying siblings not found in household censuses. Two sources: the 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable) for church marriages, and image group 007936753 (Schuylkill County marriage records 1870-1910, browse-only, personCount 0) for civil records. The date range is sized to when Doyle children would plausibly be of marriageable age. Ellen Doyle (the already-known child) can serve as an anchor: her marriage record, if found, names her parents and may list siblings as witnesses (FAN leads).

output.text_response:
**Research Plan pl_001 — Who was the father of Mikkel Nielsen Blyeberg?**

The plan was created with **nine items** across four record types, all on FamilySearch, to be executed in this order:

---

**Church Records (Stagstrup Sogn — Image Group 004130616, 1763–1814) — Browse**

1. **pli_001** — Browse for Mikkel's baptism entry (~20 Aug 1779). The baptism record names both parents directly: the most likely source of definitive parentage evidence.

2. **pli_002** — Browse for the marriage of "Niels" (the father's name, inferred from the patronymic "Nielsen") before 1779. Confirms which Niels this was and supplies the mother's maiden name.

3. **pli_003** *(FAN)* — Browse for baptisms of other children of Niels at the Blyeberg farm (~1760–1800). Sibling entries each name the same father, corroborating parentage.

---

**Census Records (FamilySearch name-searchable)**

4. **pli_004** — Search Denmark Census 1787; Mikkel (~age 8) should appear in his father's household.

5. **pli_007** — Search Denmark Census 1801; Mikkel (~age 22) may still be with, or near, the father's household.

---

**Military Levy Rolls (Thisted Amt)**

6. **pli_005** — Name search in Denmark Military Levying Rolls, 1789–1861. Levy rolls enrolled each son under his father's name — direct parentage evidence for a male subject.

7. **pli_006** *(fallback for pli_005)* — Browse Image Group 004748896 (Vestervig/Thisted Amt levy rolls, 1789–1814, 0% indexed).

---

**Probate Records (Hassing Herred, Thisted Amt)**

8. **pli_008** — Name search in Denmark Probate Indexes, 1674–1851, for "Niels" dying in Hassing Herred (~1780–1840). An estate file names all heirs, placing Mikkel as a son.

9. **pli_009** *(fallback for pli_008)* — Browse Image Group 004392710 (Hassing Herred probate records, 1690–1850).

---

**Next step:** Execute the searches, beginning with the Stagstrup parish register browse (pli_001) and the 1787 census name search (pli_004). Say "search for Mikkel's baptism" or "execute the plan" to start.

openQuestions.question: Who was the father of Mikkel Nielsen Blyeberg (b. 20 Aug 1779, Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark)?

questionStatuses.nextStep: research-plan

**Plan pl_001 created for q_001** — *"Using Kentucky death certificates, when and where did Elijah Wilkins die?"*

---

### What was established from the tree

- **Birth:** c. 1814, Kentucky
- **Residence:** 1870, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — alive at that point
- No death fact, spouse, children, or sources on file

---

### Research Plan — 7 items in sequence

| # | Type | Place | Window | Repository | Collection / Notes |
|---|------|--------|--------|------------|--------------------|
| pli_001 | Vital record | Muhlenberg Co., KY | 1870–1910 | FamilySearch | *Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970* (coll. 1804888) — pre-1911 county death register, name-searchable |
| pli_002 | Vital record | Kentucky | 1911–1925 | FamilySearch | *Kentucky Deaths, 1911–1967* (coll. 1417491) — true statewide death certificates; covers the unlikely case he survived past 1911 |
| pli_003 | Vital record | Muhlenberg Co., KY | 1852–1965 | Ancestry | *Kentucky, U.S., Death Records, 1852–1965* — fallback for pli_001 |
| pli_004 | Probate | Muhlenberg Co., KY | 1870–1910 | FamilySearch | *Kentucky Probate Records, 1727–1990* (coll. 1875188) — browse-only; administrator bonds typically name the death date within months |
| pli_005 | Census | Muhlenberg Co., KY | 1880–1900 | FamilySearch | US Federal Census 1880 & 1900 — bracket the death window (present/absent) to narrow the probate browse |
| pli_006 | Cemetery | Muhlenberg Co., KY | 1870–1910 | FindAGrave | Muhlenberg County cemeteries index — headstone transcription may supply an exact date |
| pli_007 | Probate | Muhlenberg Co., KY | 1870–1910 | KDLA | Kentucky Dept. for Libraries & Archives — fallback for pli_004 if FamilySearch browse is inconclusive |

---

### Key context

Kentucky statewide death certificates didn't begin until **1 January 1911**. Since Elijah was born c. 1814 and living in Muhlenberg County in 1870, he most likely died **before 1911** — making the county death registers and **probate records** the primary evidence sources. When a man died, the county court opened an estate, and the administrator bond typically dates the death within months.

---

**Ready to execute?** The first items (pli_001, pli_002) are name-searchable on FamilySearch → **search-records**. The Ancestry item (pli_003) → **search-external-sites**. The probate browse (pli_004) → **search-records** (browse-only).

Thomas Flynn's naturalization papers may list family members, but naturalization records rarely name children. Three independent sources already confirm parentage. Low value-add for this specific question.
St. Patrick's (Minersville) marriage register may record Patrick Flynn's 1868 marriage with parents named, corroborating the parentage already evidenced.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
